title: IV. Cana Of Galilee
paragraphs: It was very late, by monastery standards, when Alyosha returned to the hermitage; the gatekeeper let him in through a side entrance. It had already struck nine—the hour of rest after a day of such upheaval for everyone. Alyosha timidly opened the door and went into the elder's cell, where the coffin now stood. There was no one in the cell but Father Païssy, reading the Gospel alone over the coffin, and the young novice Porfiry, who, worn out by the previous night's conversation and the day's unsettling events, was sleeping the deep, sound sleep of youth on the floor of the other room. Though Father Païssy heard Alyosha come in, he didn't even glance his way. Alyosha turned right from the door, toward the corner, dropped to his knees, and began to pray.

His soul was overflowing, but with mixed feelings; no single sensation stood out clearly; instead, one drove out another in a slow, continuous rotation. But there was a sweetness in his heart, and, strange to say, Alyosha wasn't surprised by it. Once again he saw the coffin before him, the hidden dead figure so precious to him, but the weeping and piercing grief of the morning no longer ached inside him. The moment he came in he'd fallen before the coffin as before a holy shrine, but joy, joy, was glowing in his mind and in his heart. The cell's one window stood open, the air fresh and cool. "So the smell must have gotten stronger, if they've opened the window," Alyosha thought. But even this thought of the smell of decay, which had struck him as so dreadful and humiliating just hours before, no longer made him feel wretched or indignant. He began praying quietly, but soon felt he was praying almost mechanically. Fragments of thought drifted through his mind, flashed like stars and went out again at once, replaced by others. And yet a sense of wholeness reigned in his soul—something steady and comforting—and he was aware of it himself. At moments he began praying fervently, longing to pour out his gratitude and love....

But once he'd begun to pray, he'd suddenly drift off into something else, sink into thought, forgetting both the prayer and whatever had interrupted it. He started listening to what Father Païssy was reading, but, worn out with exhaustion, gradually began to doze.
"And the third day there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee," Father Païssy read. "And the mother of Jesus was there: And both Jesus was called, and his disciples, to the marriage."

"Marriage? What's that?... A marriage!" floated whirling through Alyosha's mind. "There's happiness for her too.... She's gone to the feast.... No, she didn't take the knife.... That was just a tragic turn of phrase.... Well... tragic phrases should be forgiven, they have to be. Tragic phrases comfort the heart.... Without them, sorrow would be too heavy for people to bear. Rakitin's gone off down some back alley. As long as Rakitin keeps brooding over his grievances, he'll always end up down some back alley.... But the high road... The road is wide and straight and bright as crystal, and the sun is waiting at the end of it.... Ah!... What's being read?"...
"And when they wanted wine, the mother of Jesus saith unto him, They have no wine"... Alyosha heard.

"Ah, yes, I was missing that part, and I didn't want to miss it, I love this passage: it's Cana of Galilee, the first miracle.... Ah, that miracle! Ah, that sweet miracle! It wasn't people's grief but their joy Christ came to visit—He worked His first miracle to add to people's happiness.... 'Whoever loves people loves their happiness too'—he kept repeating that, it was one of his central ideas.... 'There's no living without joy,' Mitya says.... Yes, Mitya.... 'Everything true and good is always full of forgiveness,' he used to say that too"...
"Jesus saith unto her, Woman, what has it to do with thee or me? mine hour is not yet come.
"His mother saith unto the servants, Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it"...

"Do it.... Joy, the joy of some poor, very poor people.... Of course they were poor, since they didn't even have enough wine at a wedding.... Historians write that, in those days, the people living around the Sea of Galilee were about as poor as anyone could possibly be... and another great heart, that other great being, His Mother, knew He'd come not only to make His great, terrible sacrifice. She knew His heart was open even to the plain, artless merrymaking of a handful of obscure, unlearned people, who had warmly invited Him to their humble wedding. 'Mine hour is not yet come,' He said, with a gentle smile—He must have smiled gently at her. And really, was it to keep the wine flowing at poor people's weddings that He'd come down to earth? And yet He went and did just as she asked.... Ah, he's reading again"...
"Jesus saith unto them, Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim.
"And he saith unto them, Draw out now, and bear unto the governor of the feast. And they bare it.
"When the ruler of the feast had tasted the water that was made wine, and knew not whence it was: (but the servants which drew the water knew;) the governor of the feast called the bridegroom,
"And saith unto him, Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, that which is worse; but thou hast kept the good wine until now."

"But what's this, what's this? Why is the room growing wider?... Ah, yes... It's the marriage, the wedding... yes, of course. Here are the guests, here sit the young couple, and the merry crowd, and... Where's the wise governor of the feast? But who is this? Who? The walls are receding again.... Who's that, rising from the great table? What!... Him too? But he's in the coffin... and yet he's here too. He's stood up, he sees me, he's coming this way.... God!"...

Yes, he was coming toward him, toward him, that little, thin old man, with the fine wrinkles on his face, joyful, laughing softly. There was no coffin now, and he wore the same clothes he'd worn the day before, sitting among them, when the visitors had gathered around him. His face was uncovered, his eyes were shining. How could this be? He too had been called to the feast. He too, to the marriage at Cana in Galilee....
"Yes, my dear, I'm called too, called and invited," he heard a soft voice say over him. "Why have you hidden yourself away here, out of sight? Come and join us too."
It was his voice, Father Zossima's voice. And it had to be him, since he was the one calling!
The elder took Alyosha by the hand and lifted him, and he rose from his knees.

"We're rejoicing," the little, thin old man went on. "We're drinking the new wine, the wine of a new, great gladness; do you see how many guests there are? Here are the bride and bridegroom, here's the wise governor of the feast, tasting the new wine. Why are you so amazed at me? I gave an onion to a beggar woman once, and so I'm here too. And many here have given only an onion each—only one little onion.... What are any of our deeds worth, really? And you, my gentle one, you, my kind boy, you too knew how to give a starving woman an onion today. Begin your work, dear one, begin it, gentle one!... Do you see our Sun, do you see Him?"
"I'm afraid... I don't dare look," Alyosha whispered.

"Don't be afraid of Him. He's terrible in His greatness, awesome in His majesty, but infinitely merciful. He has made Himself like us out of love, and rejoices with us. He's turning the water into wine so the guests' gladness won't be cut short. He's waiting for new guests, calling new ones ceaselessly, forever and ever.... There, they're bringing new wine. Do you see, they're carrying in the vessels...."
Something glowed in Alyosha's heart, something filled it until it ached, tears of rapture rose up from his soul.... He stretched out his hands, cried out, and woke up.

Again the coffin, the open window, the soft, solemn, measured reading of the Gospel. But Alyosha wasn't listening to the reading now. It was strange—he'd fallen asleep on his knees, but now he was on his feet, and suddenly, as though propelled forward, he crossed to the coffin in three firm, quick strides. His shoulder brushed against Father Païssy without his even noticing. Father Païssy lifted his eyes from his book for a moment, but looked away again at once, seeing that something strange was happening to the boy. Alyosha gazed for half a minute at the coffin, at the shrouded, motionless dead man lying inside it, the icon on his chest, the peaked cap with its eight-pointed cross on his head. He'd only just been hearing his voice, and that voice was still ringing in his ears. He stood listening, still expecting more words, but suddenly turned sharply and walked out of the cell.

He didn't pause on the steps either, but went quickly down; his soul, overflowing with rapture, craved freedom, space, open air. The vault of heaven, full of soft, shining stars, stretched vast and fathomless above him. The Milky Way ran in two pale streams from the zenith to the horizon. The cool, motionless, still night wrapped itself around the earth. The white towers and golden domes of the cathedral gleamed out against the sapphire sky. The gorgeous autumn flowers in the beds around the house lay sleeping until morning. The silence of earth seemed to melt into the silence of the heavens. The mystery of the earth touched the mystery of the stars....

Alyosha stood, gazed, and suddenly threw himself down onto the earth. He didn't know why he embraced it. He couldn't have said why he longed so irresistibly to kiss it, to kiss all of it. But he kissed it, weeping, sobbing, soaking it with his tears, and vowed passionately to love it, to love it forever and ever. "Water the earth with the tears of your joy, and love those tears," echoed through his soul.
What was he weeping over?

Oh! In his rapture he was weeping even over those stars shining down at him from the depths of space, and "he wasn't ashamed of that ecstasy." It seemed as though threads ran from all those countless worlds of God, linking his soul to them, and it trembled all over, "in contact with other worlds." He longed to forgive everyone, for everything, and to beg forgiveness in return. Oh, not for himself, but for all men, for everyone and everything. "And others are praying for me too," echoed again through his soul. But with every passing instant he felt, clearly and almost tangibly, that something firm and unshakable, like that vault of heaven itself, had entered his soul. It was as though some idea had taken hold of the very center of his mind—and it was for his whole life, forever and ever. He'd fallen to the earth a weak boy, but he rose a resolute champion, and he knew it, felt it, suddenly, in that very moment of ecstasy. And never, never, for the rest of his life, could Alyosha forget that moment.
"Someone visited my soul in that hour," he used to say afterward, with unshakable faith in his own words.
Within three days he left the monastery, in keeping with his elder's words, who had bidden him "go out and sojourn in the world."
